Two books whose theme is the Heptateuch (Quaestiones in Heptateuchum libri VII and Locutiones in Heptateuchum libri VII) were composed by the Bishop of Hippo in the same year 419. But there seems to be no doubt that the first work at the time was the Quaestiones, since they are referred to on several occasions in the Locutions 2, although there have been authors who have defended the simultaneous writing of both works, imagining Saint Augustine writing alternately on each book of the Heptateuch, now for the Quaestiones, now for the Locutions 3. And this opinion seems supported by the Codex Corbeiensis (the oldest of the codices), which presents in this order each of the books of the Questions and the Locutions 4. The theme is easy to establish, and is logically called for by the concern that Saint Augustine felt regarding the correct understanding of the biblical word. In 384 Saint Jerome addressed a letter to Pope Saint Damasus, begging him to intervene in a special way in the problems posed by the increasing existence of versions of the Bible. A large number of deficient, erroneous translations, when not decidedly contrary to the revealed truth, made the uncontrolled multiplication of texts dangerous. He could well say: tot enim exemplaria sunt paene quot codices. Saint Augustine himself comments that everyone who believed they had some knowledge of Greek and Latin launched themselves into the daring task of biblical translator. An attempt has been made to organize the enormous volume of versions by establishing at least two large groups: the Itala, fundamentally made up of translations of European origin, and the Afra, which encompasses those of African origin. In our introduction to the Speculum (which the reader can consult in the present volume) the problem of the translation consulted by Saint Augustine is addressed. It is evident that the Hiponense did not know in its entirety the version of Saint Jerome, later compiled under the name of Vulgate, which is why the problem of authorship of the aforementioned Speculum arises. Saint Augustine basically uses the version of the Septuagint, that of Symmachus and numerous Latin and Greek codices, which he compares in a healthy desire to explain the expressions - locutions - that may be shocking, strange, if not unintelligible, for the Latin speaker 5. And such is, in summary, the content of the Locutions. The oldest codex in which this work has been preserved is the Paris codex (Bibl. N a t. Lat. 12168), from the Corbey abbey and dating back to the 8th century. TAKEN FROM THE BOOK OF "REVISIONS", II 80 Seven books on the seven books of the Holy Scriptures - made up of the five of Moses, that of Joshua and that of the Judges - I composed, recording the locutions of each of them that are less common in our language. Readers with little experience try to find the meaning of the divine words, since it is a peculiar type of phrase. And sometimes they conceive an explanation that, although it is not really far from the truth, does not unravel what the author who wrote it had really thought. What seems clear is that he said that with a particular type of expression. In the Holy Scriptures many obscure passages are clarified if the type of locution is known. But we must know the types of utterances in which the ideas are evident, so that knowledge of them also serves as a help when they are latent and allows the attentive reader to unravel their meaning. The title of this work is Locutions of Genesis, etc., in accordance, in each case, with each of the books. Contact with a corpse was a reason for impurity for anyone, and even more so for a priest, a person who was particularly required to be pure. Moses made a bronze serpent that, seen by those who suffered from snake bites, healed by virtue of sympathetic magic. However, the cult of the serpent, widespread in Canaan, as archaeological excavations reveal, never took hold among the Israelites. The king Hezekiah of Judah (2 Sam 18:4) destroyed the image and abolished the cult. While the Israelites were in Shittim they began to interact with the Moabite women, who dragged them to worship their gods, especially Baal. Yahweh, irritated, ordered Moses to kill the apostates. A vow (neder) or a promise of abstinence (fissár) was of capital importance among the Israelites.

A vow or promise made required its unavoidable and immediate fulfillment (Deut 23:22-24). But in the case of women they were only valid if it was ratified by her father (if the young woman was single) or her husband (if she was married). Only the widow or divorced woman was free to commit herself personally.

6. And each time the Lord provided them with judges, and the Lord was with the judge (lud 2,18). With a common expression, the “and” is also unnecessary here. Indeed, it would make sense like this: “and whenever the Lord provided them with judges, the Lord was with the judge.” Note also that, going from the singular to the plural, it does not say "with the judges", but with the judge; that is, with each of the judges. 7. And it came to pass that every time a judge died and they turned and became more corrupt than their fathers (Lud 2:19). The correct expression, according to our language, could be like this: "and it came to pass that every time a judge died, they became more corrupt and corrupted again than their fathers." Even if the (first) “and” were deleted, it would make complete sense: “every time a judge died, they became more corrupt and corrupted again than their fathers”; that is, more than their parents. 8. Because this nation so broke my alliance (lud 2,20). It says so much instead of "so much", that is, "so often." 38. And Abimelech hired men for them (lud 9,4). It says "for them" instead of "with them." That is, with the seventy pesos of silver he rented 218 men. 39. Vain and disturbed men (lud 9,4). Use "vain" for "light", the opposite of "sensible." Hence it is said: I will praise you among sensible people 219. 40. And he entered his father's house in Ephrathah, and killed his brothers, the sons of Jeroboal, seventy men, on a stone (lud 9,5). He had previously said that the sons of Jeroboal—that is, of Gideon—were seventy; and now he says that he kills the seventy, even though two of them were not killed; namely: the murderer himself and Joatham, the youngest, who hid. Referring to this, he adds: and Joatham, the youngest son of Jeroboal, was saved, because he hid (lud 9,5). That is why he used the exact number for the almost exact one. 41. 1. THE WORK: TITLE, CONTENT AND PURPOSE What the title of this work means, what its purpose is and what its content is, are questions that the author of the Speculum (let's say, for the moment, Saint Augustine) answers in the introduction itself. And its basic ideas are the following. The Holy Scriptures record passages that are dogmas of faith; passages that are merely informative, due to their narrative and historical nature, and passages that dictate rules, in their double aspect: positive (pointing out what to do) and negative (specifying what not to do). Limiting your attention to this third type of passages, these in the Old Testament can be of two kinds: a) those that are not valid among Christians (e.g., the observation of the Sabbath, the celebration of the new moon, etc.); b) those others that are totally relevant for Christians and are mandatory to observe. It is these last passages - the content is further limited - that are the object of the Speculum, insofar as they "concern the exercise of a pious life and good morals." Regarding them he says: "That is why I have begun to compose this work that I have in hand, to gather, with the help of God, all those precepts, selecting them from the canonical books and grouping them so that they can easily be observed as in a mirror." Here is the meaning of the title, which will re-emerge with more or less the same meaning, content or purpose in other medieval works, such as the Speculum: "Adesto mihi verum lumen" l from the Carolingian era (and with theological content), or the Speculum peccatoris 2, dating back to the 12th-13th centuries. The recipient of this Speculum that concerns us is not the man without Christian faith (so as to instill it in him), nor is it the student of the Scriptures (so that he may subject the selected texts to analysis), but rather the lukewarm believer, "so that he may realize how much it benefits him to maintain good customs and good works, and how much he needs it." There are three arguments that Plinval exposes: 1. "The work does not include any dedication to any of the friends or regular correspondents of Saint Augustine"; and furthermore: "there is not the slightest allusion to a work of this type in the letters." 2. "Contrary to what is usual in Saint Augustine, who always uses the same set of biblical quotations, whether he takes them from a Milanese translation, or whether he himself has proceeded to revise the scriptural text inspired by the Seventy, the Speculum reproduces with disconcerting fidelity the purest Hieronymite text." This assertion, of enormous importance, supposes that, "either the "transversion" of the text was carried out—when?, by whom?—with almost infallible accuracy" (an idea that we saw defended a moment ago by Dupin, and difficult to maintain if we take into account that similar operations—for example, in Pelagius—always left traces of the primitive state); "or that Saint Augustine, suddenly and without prior explanation, turns definitively to the translation of Saint Jerome, not only for The Prophets, but also for the Exodus, the Psalms and the entire New Testament." 3. But the third argument is perhaps Plinval's most original: "the spirit in which this compilation was composed does not correspond in any way to Augustinian thought." Taking into account that, as is evident above all from De doctrina christiana and the Letter to Maximus, the spirit with which Saint Augustine invites us to approach the Scriptures is that of charity and love for God and neighbor, and that of fear and piety, and that of profound humility, it is striking that all these considerations seem totally foreign to the author of the Speculum, which is limited to a mere record of positive and negative precepts extracted from the Holy Scriptures. "It is necessary," Plinval points out, "to have read De spiritu et littera and the very clear statements of Saint Augustine against the Pelagians (Ep. 167,15; Contra II Epist. Pelag. 3,2; 4,2) to know that he placed infinitely above the positive observation of the law the spirit of prayer, penitence and piety." Plinval then examines the texts that make up the Speculum, to reach this conclusion: «Far from corresponding to Augustine's conceptions, the doctrine of the Speculum is in direct contradiction with it. On the contrary, it perfectly expresses the theories of Pelagian moralism about the prerogatives of divine law and the power of human free will.

THE VULGATE Plinval's thesis poses a serious problem since his statement implies admitting the existence, in the time of Saint Augustine, of a compilation of the hexha version by Saint Jerome of practically all the books of the Holy Scriptures. Now, as Plinval himself remembers, Saint Jerome made his translations appear in the form of successive deliveries, especially between the years 391 and 406. And it is a traditionally accepted idea that such translations were never compiled by their author to form a unitary corpus. What's more: Cassiodorus is usually attributed (and this means placing us already in the 6th century) the merit of having brought together into a unit the different books of the Bible that, translated into Latin by Saint Jerome, make up what we know today as the Vulgate. And it is the Codex Amitianus (from the seventh or early eighth century) that preserves the original Hieronymite text with greatest purity. Agreeing with Plinval's theory means, therefore, advancing the existence of a copy of the Vulgate by more or less a century. Compare the dates: Jerome, 347-420; Augustine, 354-430; Cassiodorus, 480-575. And there is an even greater point: not only should the existence of a complete unitary edition be advanced to a date prior to 430 (the date on which Saint Augustine died), but also that edition would be so faithful to Saint Jerome's version that the text of the Codex Amitianus is nothing more than a faithful and identical reproduction of it. Furthermore: the author of the Speculum not only follows to the letter that

brother text of the Amitian, but goes as far as to point out—especially in the texts of the Prophets and the Psalms—the number of verses that separate the different selected passages (we point out the slight errors in the calculation in the corresponding note). This would also mean that the structuring of Scripture by verses would predate the time of Cassiodorus. In this panorama, a striking point: given that Saint Jerome did not translate Ecclesiasticus (considered by the Church as deuterocanonical), and taking into account that in the Speculum the citations of this work are very numerous (36 pp. in Weihrich's edition), where does he take them from? According to DeBruyne 22, they reproduce a translation of African origin, much inferior, due to its mediocrity, to the one used by Saint Augustine. This being the case, it is not surprising that, in 1677, Latinius Viterbitensis 23 reached the conclusion - later followed by many - that, taking into account the Augustinian Speculum, it can be deduced that the translation of Saint Jerome was not only already disseminated in the time of the Bishop of Hippo, but was also in the hands of practically everyone. The Benedictines of San Mauro went even further by stating that Saint Augustine ended up using the Hieronimian version in preference when he discovered that it was superior to all the existing ones. And they see praise of it in the last books of the Quaestiones in Heptateuchum, and especially in book IV of De doctrina christiana, taking advantage of the quotation of a passage from the prophet Amos. What response does Plinval offer to this approach? After pointing out some details regarding the order in which certain books of the Old and New Testament appear, contrasting that offered by the Vulgate with that found in the Speculum, he reaches the following conclusion: «It is probable that this type Bible, the first copy of the future Vulgate, was found in Rome. Baal-Moloch, tribal deity of the Ammonites. Possibly at first he represented the Sun. His original name was Melek=king. Children were sacrificed to him, or simply consecrated to him. Fire played a fundamental role in his cult. Solomon (1 Sam 11,5-7) introduced his cult in Israel, and erected an altar to him on the Mount of Olives. Cf. H. So much for the passages that, from the books of Moses, we have collected as worthy of taking into account. In the books that follow - and which are titled Of Joshua, Of the Judges, Of the Kingdoms (sic) and Paralipomena "6 - the history of events is recorded more than norms of life. There are, however, in the Book of Joshua a few that I have considered appropriate not to overlook in this work of ours. V.
FROM THE BOOK OF JOSHUA

The book of Zechariah exposes seven visions of the prophet. In the fifth, alluded to here, he has a vision in which he contemplates in his spirit an enormous scroll flying. To understand the text, remember that the books were long strips rolled (volume, derived from volvo, "to roll") around an umbilkus. Cf. the two previous verses, Zach 5,1-2. There are translators and commentators who interpret these statements as written "on one side", one, and "on the other side" of the scroll, the other. Writing on both sides of a volume was rare and, of course, the idea does not emerge from the text.

All these passages are those that, taken from the four gospels, we have considered appropriate to collect in this work. As can be seen, three evangelists—Matthew, Mark and Luke—are the ones who have provided us with the greatest number of standards of life, because they reflect that facet that is described as “active.” On the other hand, John stuck more to the "contemplative" aspect, so that, although his gospel is superior to the others, we nevertheless find few moral precepts in it. Let us note that there are also very few passages that we extract from the book titled Acts of the Apostles. This is explained because its content is the history of the events on which the faith was built, and it therefore includes more examples than precepts. mei disciple Sicut dilexit me Pater, et ego dilexi uos: manete in dilectione mea. Possibly even today no new considering can be added to the small but definitive study published by D. de Bruyne in the Miscellanea Agostiniana II (Rome, 1931) p.327-340, under the title of «De octo quaestionibus ex Veteri Testament. Un écrit authéntique d'Augustin». Based on two manuscripts, G. Morin 5 had published in 1911 an unpublished treatise that ancient manuscripts and catalogs attributed to Saint Augustine. Furthermore: Morin noted 2 that it was cited not only by Eugippus in his Excerpta of the works of the Bishop of Hippo (ed. by Knoell, p.392), but also by Augustine himself in his Quaestiones in Heptateucbum 2,90 (ed. by Zycha, p.154). A year later, Morin 3 published a new manuscript—the Paris B. N. 13360—of this work, which he systematically described as apocryphal. Taking into account that, of these eight questions, the first three were published by the Maurists placed immediately behind the Septemdecim quaestiones super Mattheum, Morin thought it appropriate to divide the set of Octo quaestiones in an identical way. In his opinion, the first three would probably be authentic, just as the Septemdecim quaestiones on Matthew would probably be authentic. On the other hand, the remaining five would not be Augustinian, although they were undoubtedly prior to 419 (and, therefore, older than the first three), since they are cited in the Quaestiones in Heptateucbum. What did Morin base such a theory on? De Bruyne summarizes the arguments as follows: 1. «The paleographic tradition is not the same for both parties, A and B. A would have existed separately from the origin; later, although perhaps soon, it would have joined the Septemdecim quaestiones super Mattheum, which has a similar origin: they are two fruits of the biblical discussions of Agus1 G. In nine psalms Augustine follows a highly Gallicanized text, that is, he largely abandons his usual text to follow that of Saint Jerome. These are Psalms 77, 78, 82, 104, 105, 108, 118, 135 and 150.
